title: Bytes and Binary (authoring pilot)
objective: In this step you will be able to read a hex byte as its decimal value and as an ASCII character.
takeaway: A byte holds eight bits; the lesson's 0x41 is decimal 65 and the ASCII letter A.

units.heading: Why bytes matter
units.text: When you see 0x41 in a hex dump, that's the number 65 in decimal. It happens to be the ASCII code for the letter 'A'.

units.heading: The model
units.text: A byte is 8 bits. Each bit is either 0 or 1. So a byte can represent 2^8 = 256 different values (0-255).

units.heading: The encoding, not the letter
units.text: In decimal: 127, 69, 76, 70. In ASCII: . E L F. The first four bytes literally spell ELF.

units.heading: A real example
units.text: The ELF magic number starts with these 4 bytes: 7f 45 4c 46.

units.heading: Try it
units.text: Click on each byte to see its decimal, hex, and ASCII values.

units.heading: Retrieve
units.text: 0x41 is 4*16 + 1 = 65, and 0x41 is the ASCII code for A.

units.heading: Apply
units.text: When you see 0x41 in a hex dump, that's the number 65 in decimal.

units.heading: Connect
units.text: The ELF magic number starts with these 4 bytes: 7f 45 4c 46.

answer_key.explanation: When you see 0x41 in a hex dump, that's the number 65 in decimal.
